workload: String-keyed map (key to 32-bit int): insert all keys, then look up all keys. Askitis dataset: read 46.41 vs 105.05 ns/key (2.26x faster, derived from page data); insert with reserve 244.19 vs 309.06 ns/key (1.27x faster, derived from page data); insert without reserve 545.82 vs 554.02 ns/key (about equal); memory 1031.67 vs 2110.19 MiB (2.05x less, derived from page data).

hardware: Intel i5-5200u, 8 GB RAM; best of 20 runs (hat-trie README)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11. Stores keys as packed char arrays instead of std::string, so there is no std::pair<const Key,T> and no stable references: any modifying operation invalidates iterators, references and pointers. Rehash is slow and needs spare memory because keys are copied (cannot be moved). Default max key size 65,535 and max 2^32 elements (template parameters). Erase may delay value destruction. Default hash is std::hash<std::string_view> or FNV-1a, so a faster hash (CityHash gives about 40% faster reads per the README) must be supplied by the user. Bucket-level API is missing.
caveats: The numbers are on the hat-trie README page (the array-hash README only links to the author's blog benchmark, tessil.github.io, which is egress-blocked here and was not read). Benchmark dates from 2017: GCC 6.3, a dual-core ultrabook CPU, and the comparison set is std::unordered_map, tsl::hopscotch_map, google::dense_hash_map, spp::sparse_hash_map and the tries; absl::flat_hash_map and tsl::robin_map are not in the table, so the listed absl and robin baselines are not covered. Baseline stdlib is libstdc++ by inference (GCC on Debian), not stated outright. std::unordered_map is keyed on std::string (32 bytes minimum per key), which handicaps it on memory by design. Insert is not faster without reserve (about equal on both datasets), and lookups are slower than tsl::hopscotch_map (138.24 vs 119.49 ns/key on Wikipedia) and about equal on Askitis; dense_hash_map reads slightly faster on Askitis (43.09 ns). The README says best of 20 runs, but the gist's Makefile invokes each binary once per run, so the 20-run driver is not in the gist. Peak memory with array_map without reserve (823.54 MiB) is higher than final memory because of rehash copies. Flags were read through a WebFetch summary of the gist (twice, consistent), not a raw download (gist.githubusercontent.com is blocked).

baseline: xz (and Brotli, Zstd, Lz4, Snappy; time-series codecs Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC (sdsl dac_vector), plus LeCo and ALP per the paper)
workload: Lossless compression of 64-bit integer time series (16 datasets in the ICDE 2025 paper per search snippets): compression ratio, full decompression speed and random-access speed; the repo harness measures full decompression MB/s, random access ns per query (1e6 random indexes, 10 runs) and scan speed.
claimed_speedup: README text, no numbers on the page: NeaTS provides, simultaneously, compression ratios close to or better than the best existing compressors, a faster decompression speed, and orders of magnitude more efficient random access.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for any measurement. CMakeLists.txt sets C++23 and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -march=native -mtune=native -mfpmath=sse -mavx512f -fno-math-errno; -O9 and -funroll-loops appear only in CMAKE_C_FLAGS; no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE default is set
stars_or_usage: 13 stars; ICDE 2025 paper (Guerra, Vinciguerra, Boffa, Ferragina), pages 1579-1592
tradeoffs: Research code, GPL-3.0 (README says released for academic purposes under GPL-3.0) with sdsl-lite and sux vendored in lib/. Needs a C++23 compiler (GCC 13 or Clang 16 or newer), CMake 3.22, and Squash 0.7 for the Benchmark target. SIMD decompression uses std::experimental::simd and the build adds -mavx512f and -march=native, so binaries are not portable. Input is binary 64-bit signed integers with a user-chosen maximum residual bit width, so floating-point series must be converted to integers first. Compression (piecewise nonlinear model partitioning) is the expensive side; random access works on the compressed form without full decompression, which block-based general compressors cannot do.
caveats: Paper numbers could not be read: arXiv, IEEE and the author's talk slides are blocked here, and no PDF or result table is checked into the repo (root has LeaTS.cpp, NeaTSL.cpp, SNeaTS.cpp, main_simd.cpp, CMakeLists.txt; benchmark/ holds Chimp, Chimp128, Gorilla, TSXor sources, neats_lossless.cpp, gp_compressors_bench.hpp, st_compressors_bench.hpp; the datasets are on a d4science link not opened). What the search snippets said, not verified on any opened page: NeaTS reaches compression ratios close to xz and Brotli with up to 1 order of magnitude faster decompression and 3 orders of magnitude faster random access (talk-slide snippet); fastest decompression on 10 of 16 datasets; ratio better than Zstd by 28.49% on average, better than Lz4 by 52.77% and Snappy by 50.20%; faster compression than LeCo by 36.26% and ratio better by 12.80% on average; compared compressors Xz, Brotli, Zstd, Lz4, Snappy, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC, Gorilla, LeCo, ALP. A snippet figure of 2561.31 MB/s decompression for NeaTS next to PLA 2997.00 and AA 2420.20 appears to belong to the lossy NeaTS-L comparison against PLA and AA, so it is not used as the lossless claim. Repo evidence is thin: benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp main() currently runs only squash_scan with lz4 and has everything else commented out; main_simd.cpp prints NeaTS compression, random-access and full decompression speed but its final 'Decompression speed' line times a SIMD copy of the raw data, not NeaTS; LeCo and ALP are not in the repo harness; no CPU model or build flags are given. The README's plain 'cmake ..' sets no optimization level for C++ code (only the C flags have -O9), so a default build is unoptimized unless -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release is passed. Tier C is a placeholder: the paper is peer reviewed (B), and A is possible if it states CPU, compiler and flags since the comparator harness is public; retier when arXiv 2412.16266 or the IEEE page is readable.
